entry.title: I Found the Best Plastic-Free Coffee Brewers, Including Drip Machines
entry.summary: Eliminating plastic from your coffee routine is difficult but not impossible. Here’s some gear to help you get there, including drip machines.
entry.content:
Brewing coffee without plastic is not difficult — a stovetop percolator does a fine job preparing pre-ground supermarket beans. However, brewing a high-quality cup at a reasonable price without sacrificing convenience turns out to be surprisingly challenging. Most of the drip machines we’ve tested contain some plastic, even the expensive ones. That’s because the prevalence of plastic in coffee equipment has as much to do with its performance as with its low cost.

Pastime Coffee owner-operator Justin Dedini explained that a plastic Hario V60 was his preferred pour-over method for many years because the material is better at retaining heat in the brewer — crucial for extracting the delicate, fruity, and floral flavors people look for in craft coffee. Then one day, after years of exposure to hot water, his trusty plastic cone began crumbling into the coffee he’d been brewing. “That was when it really hit me that it may not be the healthiest option,” said Dedini. His search for alternatives led him to develop better methods of brewing with ceramic, metal, and glass drippers, which are great if you have the time and patience for them. He has yet to find an automatic coffee maker that meets his requirements.

I then asked Lance Hedrick, one of YouTube’s most prolific coffee-equipment reviewers, but he’d arrived at the same conclusion: “If you go the drip-coffee-maker route, you’re going to have plastic somewhere touching water.” Hedrick explained that pour-over is easier but warned that even manual methods aren’t plastic free if the interior of your water kettle contains plastic parts. To my surprise, I discovered this to be true of the Bonavita kettle I’d been using for many years. Espresso machines tend to be better about avoiding plastic parts in areas that get hot, but Hedrick cautioned that they can get quite expensive and that a high price is no guarantee: “Even higher-end, $4,000 machines can have plastic intake tubes and water tanks.”

Regardless of brewing method, the closer I looked, the more plastic I found. Bodum French presses may appear to be made of steel and glass, but the lids on most models have a built-in strainer made from black plastic. A Technivorm Moccamaster’s glass carafe and metal body provide an elegant foil for the plastic it has everywhere else. The list goes on, but I did eventually manage to find and test some notable exceptions, which I have grouped below by brewing method. I also have recommendations for grinders and kettles.

Updated on November 27, 2026
We added recommendations for the latest Simply Good Coffee Plastic-Free Brewers and the stainless-steel Aeropress. We’ve also updated our plastic-free coffee gear with the latest pricing and availability.

I recommend this set to anyone looking for an easy, tasty, and consistent way to make pour-over coffee for two. The tall, narrow shape ensures that any water poured into the top makes its way through more of the coffee as it drips downward. This provides even extraction and balanced flavor, even if your pours aren’t perfectly timed or placed. And unlike other flat-bottom drippers I’ve tried, the holes never clog before brewing is finished. It’s also one of Dedini’s favorites because his tests involving multiple temperature probes found the double-walled stainless-steel design has better heat retention than his old plastic dripper.

The dripper and insulated glass carafe are available separately, but I recommend getting them as a set because the dripper is too narrow to fit on most other carafe designs.

This classic has a convenient all-in-one design and makes a healthy shareable portion of light-bodied, fruit-forward coffee. However, its thick paper filters absorb some of the toastier, chocolatey notes, so it’s not the best choice for fans of medium- or dark-roast coffees. (Switching to a reusable stainless-steel filter can help with this, even if it’s kind of annoying to clean.) And its lack of insulation means coffee gets cold pretty quickly after it’s brewed.

Appearances can be deceiving when it comes to plastic content in French presses. For example, I confirmed with customer support that this highly rated Public Goods press that appears to be made entirely of glass and steel uses plastic parts to attach the filter to the plunger. Hario’s French press costs a bit more, but I confirmed with specialty-coffee-equipment retailer Prima Coffee that it has no plastic parts. For a more classic look, there’s also a wood-handled version.

This insulated French press is our heirloom-quality pick because of its 100 percent stainless-steel construction. Kelsey Horwitz of Beacon Coffee calls it the gold standard of French presses because in addition to making great coffee, Frieling sells all the replacement parts you could need to keep it going forever.

A longtime favorite among coffee aficionados, now in a plastic-free stainless-steel design. I was never convinced that the fragile, $200 glass version was a good buy, but this sturdier version feels like a better value. I tested it against the original, and as long as you take the time to preheat the insulated stainless-steel brewing chamber, it produces coffee that’s every bit as good as the original plastic version. At 1.4 pounds, it’s nearly three times heavier than the original, so I can’t recommend it for travel.

The Weber BIRD is my top gift recommendation for the coffee nerd who has it all. It’s a “zero bypass” brewer, which means all the water that goes into the device is forced through all of the coffee grounds inside. The Aeropress is the most popular brewer in this category, but it is made almost entirely of plastic. Although Aeropress recently released a $200 glass-and-steel version, it’s difficult to use and I can’t recommend it. Meanwhile, the experience of brewing with the BIRD is so delightful that the quality of the coffee — which is excellent — is almost beside the point. It feels more like playing with an overengineered German children’s toy than brewing coffee.

While French presses separate grinds from brew by plunging them to the bottom, the BIRD pulls them up slowly as you twist the precision-machined brass wing nut around the polished steel driveshaft. The rising filter has a silicone seal around it that generates a vacuum in its wake, sucking the brewed coffee into the bottom of the carafe. The seal releases with a muted thunk once the filter reaches the wider lip of the carafe. This allows you to lift both the lid and the spent grinds away, leaving behind a bright, flavorful, and grit-free serving of coffee.

If you prefer a stronger cup of coffee but don’t want to mess around with espresso, a Mokapot is another all-metal stovetop option worth considering. I’m going to venture a guess that anyone who’s concerned about plastic in their coffee might also be avoiding aluminum cookware, so I’d recommend Bialetti’s induction-ready stainless-steel version instead of the classic design. The “six-cup” version brews about one American mug of coffee at a time.

Hedricks told me plastic-free espresso is more easily achievable than a drip machine because of manufacturers like La Pavoni, whose lever-actuated designs predate the widespread adoption of plastics. In a machine such as the Europiccola, water goes directly into the boiler, eliminating the need for a plastic tank. And since you provide the pressure with your arm strength, there’s no need for a pump or any water lines.

If you want a machine with a pump, you’ll have to accept a plastic water reservoir. (Hedrick told me about a new $8,000 Swiss machine with an all-stainless-steel water path, but it’s not widely available for purchase yet.) If you can accept cold water touching plastic, Hedrick recommends the Gaggia Classic Pro as an affordable and capable option with a mostly metal water path, aside from two silicone water lines. Unlike cheaper machines, it’s completely serviceable if anything goes wrong.

This is the latest version of the first drip machine with a completely plastic-free (and aluminum-free) brewing path, from the glass water reservoir through the stainless-steel internals and all the way to the carafe (also glass). It may look like a Moccamaster, but it’s actually better at brewing coffee thanks to an automatic bloom mode, which pre-wets the coffee before brewing begins, and a wider circular showerhead that promotes even extraction. The metal internals and brew basket conduct more heat away from the water than plastic parts would, so the brewing temperature ends up being a bit lower than ideal for some lighter roasts. But overall, it’s a very impressive and consistent brewer that I’d recommend to anyone looking to minimize plastic exposure in their morning routine.

There’s now a programmable version of the same great machine for people who don’t mind pre-grinding their coffee and want to wake up to a fresh pot.

If you prefer a larger-capacity coffee maker, or are looking for a more modern aesthetic, senior writer Emma Wartzman recommends the Caraway ten-cup coffee maker for its simple, one-button interface and excellent results: The coffee “tastes clean, balanced, and full-bodied every time — just as much as with the OXO that is our best overall pick and the one that has been in my own kitchen for the last few years.”

The easiest way to ensure your coffee isn’t touching plastic while it’s being ground or shortly thereafter is to use a manual grinder. The Timemore C2S is a popular, well-reviewed option that’s well under $100. It can grind up to 25 grams of beans at a time and, unlike most options in this price range, even the lid is made of metal.

Hedrick is also a fan of Timemore’s electric grinders, and I was able to confirm with customer support that the Sculptor series has an all-steel grind path as well as a metal cup for receiving ground coffee — though whole beans do touch a plastic hopper on their way into the machine. The more affordable 064S features swappable 64-mm. flat burrs and is suitable for pour-over and espresso use.

If you’d rather not even have your whole beans touch any plastic, then the Zerno Z1 is a truly plastic-free grinder from the hopper to the chute — even if it costs well over $1,000. Hedrick praises the grind quality of these grinders and likes that they’re made in Chicago, but she laments that there’s always a long wait list to order one. Dedini is also a Zerno fan and plans to order the commercial-grade Z2 when it becomes available.

I must confess that I don’t personally love the Fellow kettle’s dial interface, which feels fussy compared with the buttons on my trusty Bonavita of nearly a decade. But after Hedrick mentioned that some stainless-steel kettles actually have plastic on the inside, I took a look and discovered that my Bonavita uses a plastic part on the inside of the kettle to attach the handle to the body. It’s located above the maximum fill line, but it’s still exposed to heat and condensation. Meanwhile, I was able to confirm with Fellow that the only non-stainless part on the inside of the kettle is a small silicone gasket to hold and protect the temperature sensor. So if you’re looking to avoid plastic in your gooseneck kettle, go with the Fellow.

If you’d rather not deal with a silicone gasket, get a stovetop kettle. Hario’s V60 Buono has a wider base than most and is induction compatible. Its rounded spout doesn’t pour as precisely as the Fellow or Bonavita electric kettles, but it is truly plastic free on the inside.

entry.content:

Sometimes the very best Black Friday deals are on practical luxuries, like a really good detangling hairbrush that might otherwise seem too pricey. The Bur Bur Mermaid Mini Wet Detangling Brush, which is currently 30 percent off, is one such deal. It’s a favorite of multiple Strategist staffers who praise the “stimulating” quality of the nylon bristles and its efficacious detangling powers. Strategist senior editor Jen Trolio owns multiple Bur Bur brushes and says she would happily add another Mermaid detangling brush to her family’s collection, since she and her two long-haired daughters are constantly stealing them from one another.

entry.title: It’s Black Friday at Brooklinen, and Everything Is at Least 25 Percent Off
entry.summary: Including some of our all-time favorite pillows, sheets, and towels.
entry.content:
Since holiday gift-shopping season doesn’t technically start until after Thanksgiving, I say you’re free to use early Black Friday sales as an excuse to treat yourself — and one of the best, most self-care-y ways to do that is with some fresh linens, specifically from Brooklinen. The brand’s sale is on now: Everything is 25 percent off, and bundles are up to 40 percent off. There’s no shortage of great stuff to buy, so I’ve created a very digestible 15-item list below, much of which is culled from our best-of-brand roundup. The discounts will stick around through December 2, but there are some really excellent new colors and patterns to choose from this year, and I’m betting most of those won’t stay in stock nearly as long as staple colors like blue and gray.

As always, make sure to sign up for the Strategist Deal Freaks Daily newsletter to receive each day’s best deals in your inbox (as well as sales just for newsletter subscribers). And if you want even more, sign up for our regular email newsletter for tons more newsletter exclusives.

Brooklinen’s percale duvet cover is our pick for the best duvet cover overall. Senior writer (and our resident bedding expert) Lauren Ro says it’s smooth, lightweight, and breathable and has “a delicious crispiness that you can almost hear.” Senior editor Winnie Yang also loves it — her daughter has been using it for over four years, and Yang notes that “the percale is smooth and soft” and “feels cool and never clammy.” (Percale is also known to be one of the best weaves for hot sleepers.) The brand’s coordinating percale sheet set is also Strategist-approved.

If you want something silkier, this sateen set, which also has a spot on our Best in Class sheets guide, is perfect. Ro has some and says they’re among the softest sheets she owns and they “only get better with time.” There’s a coordinating duvet cover for these, too.

These linen sheets are a favorite of sleep experts, interior designers, and Strategist staffers alike. Ro says they’re the gauziest of all the linen sheets she has tried, and lead editor Lauren Levy said they made her “fall in love with linen sheets” because they have “an immediately worn-in feel that only gets softer over time.” This bundle includes everything you need to dress your bed: a duvet cover, a flat sheet, a fitted sheet, and four pillowcases. There are multiple color combinations to choose from, including the beautifully eye-catching autumnal plaid above.

Brooklinen’s all-season down comforter is one of the best down comforters we’ve tried. It also comes in light- and heavyweight options, and all three are perfect for anyone who wants the cloudlike experience of a down comforter without having to pay a premium price. Their down-alternative option is also one of our favorites across the board. It’s ideal for vegans, folks with allergies, and anyone hoping to save some money on bedding, and it can be used without a duvet cover thanks to a smooth-to-the-touch cotton-sateen finish.

Adjustable pillows are ideal for anyone who struggles to find a pillow that meets their personal support and firmness preferences. This one is Strategist approved. It’s also so easy: Instead of manually removing or adding fill (so tedious!), it adjusts via zippers that run along the long ends. When both are zipped, the pillow will be slightly firmer and feel more dense; when both are unzipped, the pillow will be slightly fluffier, softer, and easier to sink into.

This 100 percent mulberry-silk pillowcase made former deals writer Alexandra Polk believe in the power of sleeping on silk. “It never sticks to my face after I’ve slapped on my skin care, and it’s incredibly soft but not slick,” she wrote. It comes in solid colors and patterns — and speaking of the latter, it’s also our favorite patterned silk pillowcase. Writer Tembe Denton-Hurst notes that it “feels elevated in comparison to some other styles I’ve seen, while maintaining a high-quality fabric composition.”

Writer Bella Druckman says this mask is perfect for anyone who wants to doze off under a cover of pure silk without splurging. “It’s soft, slightly larger than the Slip mask, and loose enough that it doesn’t give me headaches despite not having an adjustable strap,” Druckman writes.

This is the best women’s bathrobe we’ve tested and our favorite (less expensive) robe for men. It’s supremely giftable but also perfect if you’re looking to get yourself a little something special.

The most giftable item on this list: an extremely fluffy blanket.

These are the best heavyweight bath towels we’ve found. They’re sumptuously lofty and extremely absorbent, and the long-staple Turkish cotton is woven in a zero-twist loop that makes them very soft. (Twisted fibers create a rougher hand.) They come in two- and four-piece sets and a bunch of really pretty solid and striped colors.

For something lighter in weight, try this 100 percent Turkish-cotton waffle style. The four-piece bundle can be split into two sets of two so you can mix and match colors and patterns.

entry.content:
For the Strategist team, gift scouting is a year-round sport. That means by April, we had already reviewed the newest (and most affordable) MacBook, and in July, we ID’d Erling Haaland’s hair ties right off his man bun. Now that it’s officially holiday season, we’re filling our signature lineup of gift guides with the most surprising and delightful gifts from our research, reviews, and hundreds of interviews with hard-to-shop-fors (think tween girls and, well, husbands).

Consider the below a highlight reel of every single gift guide that we’ve written (so far) this season. I’ve handpicked all the most worth-it items that have appeared in our gift guides for everyone on your list, whether it’s your wellness-obsessed mom, ever-confusing teen cousin, or 5-year-old niece who wants nothing more than a Tin Can. And as we inch closer to Christmas, I’ll be regularly updating this article with even more gifts from all our latest guides, so I suggest bookmarking this post to stay up-to-date.

If you’re new here, I also recommend signing up for our newsletter to get even more of our holiday coverage straight to your inbox. Between our predictions about the trendiest gifts for different age groups and the return of The Strategist Gifting Game, there’s so much to look forward to.

Now that every beauty brand on the map has made its own Advent calendar, we’ve gotten choosier with the ones we feel are actually worth it (as in, not just full of samples). Find all of our favorite beauty Advent calendars here.

Now that adults can treat themselves to 24 days of wine, lipstick, and tinned fish, Advent calendars that are actually for kids don’t get the same spotlight. To help you sift through the noise for age-appropriate ones, writer Liza Corsillo found more than 60 options for toddlers to teens. Find more Advent calendars for kids here.

When shopping for her mom, Strategist senior writer Ambar Pardilla likes to go for something she needs but hasn’t gotten around to buying or something she would never, ever buy for herself. Find all the gifts that fit that description here.

When shopping for her wife (or anyone, really), Strategist writer Tembe Denton-Hurst employs a core strategy: mixing highbrow and lowbrow. We suggest stuffing a makeup bag with some fancy hand soap, but Denton-Hurst compiled more than 50 other ideas. Find them all here.

When looking for a gift for your mother-in-law, you want to find something she’ll actually use and doesn’t already have. Pardilla compiled all the gifts that fit the bill here.

When shopping for a college student, it’s hard to go wrong with one of the water bottles or plushies that’s getting some buzz on campus. Our gift guide for college students includes tons of the latest products taking over teen and 20-something wish lists plus some tried-and-true dorm essentials. Find all of them here.

When shopping for 1-year-olds, Corsillo says it’s best to buy toys that encourage them to move their bodies and explore new sensory experiences. She chatted with child-development professionals, art therapists, tasteful parents, and toy-trend experts about their top picks and put them all into her gift guide for these curious toddlers. The best gifts for 2-year-olds, though, “often focus on the ways they can have an impact, accomplish a goal, or solve a problem,” Corsillo says. “They’re also practicing their language skills and learning how to socialize, often through pretend play.” Find more gifts for these energetic 2-year-olds here.

entry.title: How to Shop Black Friday and Cyber Monday, According to Our Deals Editor
entry.summary: A cheat sheet to navigating the best sales of the year.
entry.content:
Black Friday and Cyber Monday are without a doubt the best days of the year for sales. I should know — I write about sales all year long. Many retailers offer a 20 percent discount here and there throughout the year, but Black Friday is when they really let loose and increase that discount to 30 or 40 percent in a bid for your attention at the shoppiest time of all. If you approach these sales smartly, you can get all of your holiday shopping done early and below budget — and don’t forget about treating yourself.

Black Friday 2026 takes place on November 27, and runs through Monday, November 30, so you have some time to prepare. Sometimes it pays to shop early, before things sell out. Other times it pays to wait for a slightly better discount to come around. To help you navigate the sales, I’ve racked my deals-obsessed brain to come up with a list of tips, including which categories have the best deals, which you can safely skip, which deals tend to sell out fastest, and more.

Last year, we made it possible to save products on our site and see them in your account. I’d use that tool to start making your shopping list now. That way, when Black Friday rolls around, you can simply go to your account, see what’s on sale, and shop from there. Even better: Sign up for email notifications when something you’ve saved goes on sale. Black Friday sales often start long before the actual day, so the earlier you start saving products, the earlier you can start saving money.

One of my recently saved products, which I’m hoping will go on sale for Black Friday, is hydrating shower oil. (Crucial for winter!) “Along with its delicate floral scent, I love that the Bioderma has a gentle and fine lather, which washes away cleanly without any oily residue, so there’s no need to double-cleanse,” says writer Brenley Goertzen, who wrote our guide to the best bodywashes.

Shipping times are notoriously finicky this time of year, so it’s a good idea to order your gifts as early as possible. I suggest spending the weeks before Black Friday and Cyber Monday making a list of possible gifts for people on your list (and saving them to your account!), so when the sales go live, you can quickly check to see what’s on sale. And again, I’d do this sooner than later, as the deals have already started, and they’re already worth shopping.

If you need gift ideas, we’ve got plenty, and we’ll be finding all the best on-sale gifts now through Cyber Monday, so stay tuned for more. (I’d also recommend signing up for our Deal Freaks Daily newsletter, where we’ll be sharing all of our on-sale gift picks this holiday season.)

One year, I went into Black Friday shopping with the goal of finding the best deal I could on AirPod Pros. And find them I did, and for a respectable 24 percent off. It was one of only a few things I bought over the weekend.

Black Friday sales now begin early in November and ramp up through the month. For the most part, the deals that go live before Black Friday are the same as what you get during actual Cyber Week. There’s no way to be totally sure, but my rule of thumb: If the brand is smaller and calling the sale just a Black Friday or Cyber Week sale, it’s probably not going to change between now and Cyber Monday. If it’s a bigger retailer like Amazon and Nordstrom, and it’s calling the sale an early Black Friday sale (or something other than simply Black Friday), the deals probably will change closer to Black Friday. That doesn’t mean the early deals are bad; it’s just likely that new deals will be added to the mix.

All to say, in general, if there’s something you really want and it’s already on sale, get it while it’s in stock. If you don’t think the item will sell out, you can wait. There are a few cases where the deal is a bit better — like 25 percent off instead of 20 percent — come actual Black Friday.

Expensive items will be at their best prices on Black Friday — and shoppers no longer have to camp outside a JCPenney or Walmart in order to buy a washing machine or TV on sale. The deals have simply moved online, where you can find the best discounts of the year on appliances and tech. Best Buy and Target are both good places to start, especially if you’re looking for Apple tech or even a high-end vacuum. Some of these brands still have online doorbusters that only last a short amount of time, but they typically advertise them in advance, so you can plan ahead.

Our pick for the best noise-canceling headphones overall was on sale for October Prime Day for over $80 off. It should have a similar discount (if not slightly better) for Black Friday.

When people ask writer Jordan McMahon what they should wait to buy until Black Friday, his answer is always tech. Specifically, expensive tech like headphones, tablets, and gaming consoles. “You probably won’t find a better deal than the ones offered this week,” he says. Last year, we saw great deals at individual retailers like JBL, Sonos, and Dyson, as well as tons of discounts at such megaretailers as Best Buy, Amazon, and Target.

Tech is a category you should definitely check for price matching, though. Apple doesn’t discount its products on its own site, but it sometimes offers gift cards of varying amounts with the purchase of a product. Target, Best Buy, and Amazon, however, offer straight-up discounts on Apple products. The best place to buy depends on what you want — money now or later — but it’s worth comparing and considering before paying.

“Amazon always has significant discounts on its own products, like Kindles and Echo devices — I always wait until this time of year when I need to upgrade one of my e-readers,” McMahon says.

Sadly, the prices of streaming services just keep going up. Last year, we saw several streaming services offer more than half-off monthly subscription fees. If you’ve been unsure whether another streaming service is worth it, now is a good time to subscribe and try it out cheaply, often for a whole year. (These make a nice gift, too.)

As is usually the case during holiday sales, tons of clothes are significantly discounted. Last year, Madewell offered 40 percent off sitewide, and Alex Mill’s Black Friday sale was a surprise hit with Strategist readers and staffers alike. The sheer volume can be a bit overwhelming, though, which is why our senior fashion writer Ambar Pardilla will be sniffing out what’s actually a good deal. As she’s done in years past, she’ll be rounding up her best finds, organized by retailer, making it easy to compare discounts and find the very best ones.

One category I look forward to in the fashion sphere each Black Friday is the on-sale cashmere, and I’m sure this time around will be no diffferent.

According to senior writer Liza Corsillo, the big three — Amazon, Target, and Walmart — have the most sprawling deals on toys during Black Friday. Last year, she found dozens of options for over 50 percent off at these stores. But don’t limit yourself to just those three: Smaller, independent brands like Fat Brain Toys and Maisonette, for instance, had good (and sometimes even better) discounts, too, with up to 60 or 70 percent off certain toys.

A lot of beauty brands discount products by up to 20 percent throughout the year, but they almost always bump that discount up to 25 or 30 percent off for Black Friday. “I always use it as an opportunity to stock up on my favorite beauty products, buy gifts for loved ones, and try out new products I’ve been eyeing throughout the year,” says beauty writer Tembe Denton-Hurston. It’s a particularly good time to shop at Sephora: Last year, it offered up to 50 percent off brands like Augustinus Bader, Glossier, and Verb, and there were flash deals that changed daily. Also good to grab? Stocking stuffers like lip gloss, nail polish, and pimple patches.

Mattresses are always on sale. While a typical discount at any given time is about 15 to 20 percent off, Black Friday seems to be one of the only times mattress brands bump up the savings, usually by an extra 5 percent. (Those deals usually start well before Black Friday, so you don’t have to wait to get a better price.)

Retailers like Amazon, Nordstrom, and Target will often price-match the deals going on at other sites. This can make shopping easier because they’ll generally have faster and cheaper shipping and/or a more flexible return window, which is especially great for gift returns.

Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales vary from brand to brand, but in my experience, most places don’t increase discounts on Cyber Monday. At most, they might throw in a freebie with your purchase or add more items to the sales bin, but usually the discount is the same. So my advice here is the same as what I offered above: If you really want something, buy it early. If you’re willing to gamble on stock, you can wait and see if a discount changes or a freebie is added to the mix.

Yes, all the big brands will have sales, but so do smaller businesses — and they often don’t wait for Small Business Saturday to go live. Salter House never has sales, but I bought this nightdress while it was a rare 20 percent off on Black Friday a few years ago.

If this year is anything like the past few, a fair amount of retailers will extend their sales and turn the entire first week of December into a full-on Cyber Week. The discounts won’t change from Cyber Monday, but brands might throw in a free gift with purchase to persuade you to check out.
